title: Can AI inventory management free up cash without more stockouts?
description: AI inventory management for distributors and manufacturers: what it changes, what your ERP already does, and how much cash a 10% stock cut frees.
verdict: Cash is the prize: machinery distributors hold 81 days of sales in stock, often costing 20%+ a year to carry[^1][^4].
Check your ERP first: NetSuite now sets safety stock by segment; Business Central still takes it by hand[^25][^27].
Buyers keep approving every order; log their overrides, which cut profit 5.77% in one parts-retailer field test[^8][^9].
Fix stock records before any model: one study found 65% wrong, and small errors can stall automatic reordering[^17][^18].
Supplier deliveries have slowed 11 months running; machine-learned lead times cut stock 7% at equal service in one study[^3][^13].

summary: AI inventory management resets each item's safety stock and reorder point from real demand and supplier lead times[^25][^13]. What changes: buyers approve suggested orders instead of building them; one store study cut managers' ordering time 36.5%[^11]. Clean stock records and honest lead times make or break it[^17][^15].
humanRole: The buyer keeps it: they approve every suggested purchase order and transfer before it goes out[^11][^8]. They log a reason for each override, since overrides of one parts retailer's stocking tool cut profit 5.77%[^8][^9].

Planner or inventory analyst: sets the service level (the share of orders filled from stock) for each segment, and owns lead-time and demand inputs[^25][^23]. Adjusting the tool's inputs, not its outputs, raised profit 4.92% in a later field test[^10].
Branch or warehouse manager: accepts or rejects each transfer suggestion, and recounts the items the system flags[^21][^17].

Controller: decides markdown, return or scrap for flagged dead stock before year end[^35][^36]. A flag alone creates no tax write-down; the goods must be scrapped or offered at a lower price[^35][^37].
teamAfter: Buyers work a ranked list of exceptions (stockout risk, excess, late orders) instead of scanning every item, and planners tune the inputs[^11][^10]. In one store-chain study, ordering time fell 36.5% while service rose 2.9%[^11].
Buyers spend more time chasing suppliers: at one machinery maker, about 14% of orders arrived late[^14]. Lead-time models flag those orders early, but only roughly[^15].
Planners review the override log each month against results, and adjust inputs where a supplier or item has changed[^10][^8].
Among US firms where AI changed tasks, 66% use it only to help staff; 2% report AI-related falls in employment[^12].

example.input: A parts distributor with $40M of sales and three branches. At the machinery-distributor ratio of 2.65, it holds about $8.8M of stock[^1]. The pilot reads 24 months of sales by item and branch, plus each supplier's order and receipt dates.
example.output: Safety stock per item from measured supplier lead times, dead-stock flags at 180 and 365 days, and transfer suggestions a branch manager approves. A 10% stock cut would free about $880k and save $88k-$265k a year to carry, 0.2-0.7% of sales[^5][^4]. Buyers approve every order and transfer.

tables.title: What does AI change in each stock decision?
tables.intro: It recalculates safety stock, reorder points, segments, dead-stock flags and branch transfers from your own demand and lead times, instead of fixed ERP settings[^24][^13]. Each row compares a typical ERP setting with what an AI planning tool does instead[^27]. Features vary by vendor, so ask which rows a tool really recalculates[^16].

recipes.name: 1. Start here: lead-time and dead-stock checks on your own history
recipes.when: Firms with an analyst who can work an ERP export. Buyers' reported lead times for production materials rose six days in a year, so old settings may run short[^3].
flow: Analyst: export purchase-order lines with order date, receipt date and supplier
Analyst: work out each supplier's average lead time and spread, and compare with the ERP field
Buyer: review the outliers and update the ERP
Analyst: list items with no sale in 180 or 365 days and over 12 months of cover
Buyer: choose return, transfer, markdown or scrap for each
Controller: sign off any write-down before year end
recipes.cost: Mostly analyst time, with no new licence. Keep it narrow: internal builds reached deployment about half as often as outside partnerships, in MIT NANDA's 2025 report[^40].

recipes.name: 2. One warehouse on NetSuite or Business Central: tune what you own
recipes.when: Single-site firms whose ERP already holds clean sales and order history. NetSuite 2026.2 sets safety stock by segment; Business Central needs it typed in[^25][^27].
flow: Planner: export 24 months of sales and purchase-order dates
Planner: sort items into ABC (value) and XYZ (demand swings) classes
Ops head: set a target service level for each class
Planner: switch on Inventory Optimization, or set reorder rules by class in Business Central
Buyer: approve suggested orders each week and log each override with a reason
Ops head: after 12 weeks, compare stock and fill rate with the same weeks last year
recipes.cost: Mostly your planner's time. The features sit inside the ERP you already pay for[^25][^28].

recipes.name: 3. Several branches and thousands of parts: a planning add-on
recipes.when: Distributors with branches, lumpy spare parts or many suppliers. Transfers between branches pay most where moving stock is cheap next to holding it[^20][^22].
flow: Ops head: shortlist two add-ons that connect to your ERP
Planner: give each vendor the same 24 months of history
Vendor: replay last year under its suggested settings
Planner: check the replay against what really happened
Branch manager: approve or reject suggested transfers before any new order
Buyer: approve orders; planner reviews overrides monthly
recipes.cost: Smart IP&O lists from $695 a month on Capterra[^33]; EazyStock quotes only[^34]. Vendors claim 6-12 weeks to go live: Netstock 6-10, StockIQ about 12[^41][^42].

ownData.title: How much cash sits in stock in your sector?
ownData.intro: These figures are as of September 2026[^1][^2]. We turned Census inventories-to-sales ratios (months of sales in stock) into cash; times 30.4 gives days, and a 10% cut frees a tenth. Carrying cost is that stock times 10-30% a year, from APQC's 10% median to a 30% textbook rate[^5][^4]; use your own rate[^6].
ownData.note: Pulled 26 Nov 2026; national averages for all firm sizes, seasonally adjusted but not price-adjusted, so not a mid-size benchmark[^1][^2]. Stock is at cost and sales at selling price, and manufacturer rows use shipments. Ratios fell partly because wholesale sales grew 19.8% in a year while stock grew 7.6%[^1].

rules.name: Treasury Regulation 1.471-2(c), subnormal goods
rules.what: Damaged, shop-worn or obsolete goods can be valued below cost for tax when actually offered for sale at the lower price[^35]. The offer must come within 30 days after the inventory date[^35]. Time dead-stock flags so you can act before year end.

rules.name: IRS practice unit, lower of cost or market
rules.what: Excess or overstock is not subnormal unless it is scrapped or actually offered at reduced prices[^36]. A tool's dead-stock list is a prompt to act, not a write-down[^36].

rules.name: Thor Power Tool Co. v. Commissioner, 439 U.S. 522
rules.what: The court disallowed a tax write-down of excess spare parts still held for sale at full price[^37]. Keeping the old price while writing the stock down does not work for tax.

rules.name: FASB ASU 2015-11, Inventory (ASC 330)
rules.what: For FIFO or average-cost inventory, your books carry it at the lower of cost and net realizable value[^38]. Your accountant sets any reserve; this page is not tax or accounting advice.

howToTest: Check your counts, replay last year on the tool, then pilot one branch: start by cycle-counting a random sample of about 200 item-locations[^17]. If many records are wrong, fix counting before you test any tool.
Pull 24 months of demand by item and location, plus each purchase order's order, promised and receipt dates. Add today's ERP safety stock, reorder point and lead time.
Measure each supplier's real lead time against the ERP field, and count late order lines[^14][^24].
Sort items into ABC by value and XYZ by demand swings: X under 50% variation, Y 50-100%, Z over 100%[^23].

Replay the last 12 months twice on the same demand: once with today's settings, once with the tool's. Compare average stock value, fill rate (share of order lines shipped complete) and number of orders[^13].
Then run it live on one branch or product family for 8-12 weeks, with buyers approving, beside a matched branch. Log every override with a reason code[^8][^10].
Price the result in cash and service: stock-to-sales ratio, fill rate, dead-stock value and buyer hours. Compare your ratio with your sector in our table above[^1].
Ask each vendor to run the replay on your data before you sign anything.
watchOuts: It goes wrong on bad stock records, lumpy parts, rough lead-time guesses, costly overrides and branch averages that hide problems[^17][^26]. Each fix is below.
Wrong stock records feed wrong orders: one study found 65% of 370,000 store records inaccurate[^17]. Undetected losses can freeze automatic reordering, so recount flagged items first[^18][^19].
Lumpy parts break the maths. NetSuite warns its results are approximate for intermittent, promotional or seasonal demand, so review those items by hand[^26].
Lead-time predictions are useful, not precise: one model explained only 30-55% of the variation[^15]. Keep a buyer's judgment on top and refresh lead times often[^15][^3].
Overrides can cost money: on mature and declining items they hurt profit in a field test[^8]. Log every override and review the log against results[^9].
Much of the research behind these tools ignores lead time: most papers in a 2025 review assumed it was zero[^16]. Ask each vendor how its model treats lead time.
Averages hide branches: Business Central's AI forecast adds up all locations and variants[^29]. Check each branch's numbers before you trust a transfer or order.

faq.q: Is AI inventory management just reorder points with a new name?
faq.a: Not always: real AI planning recalculates safety stock per item from demand and lead-time swings, while some tools keep a fixed default[^25][^24]. Ask how often it recalculates. A fixed days-of-cover default is not that[^24].

faq.q: Do we need new AI inventory management software, or does our ERP do this?
faq.a: Use your ERP for a single warehouse with steady demand; buy a planning add-on for several branches, lumpy parts or many suppliers[^25][^28][^26]. NetSuite 2026.2 sets safety stock by segment, while Business Central and Acumatica need it typed in by hand, which add-ons automate[^25][^27][^31][^32].

faq.q: How much cash could a 10% stock cut free?
faq.a: A tenth of your stock value: about $221k per $10M of sales for a typical machinery distributor, by our math from Census ratios[^1]. Carrying savings then add 10-30% of that each year, depending on your rate[^5][^4].

faq.q: What carrying cost rate should we use?
faq.a: Start from 10% to 30% a year[^5][^4], but work out your own rate, item by item if you can[^6]. APQC's median across 6,468 organizations is 10%, while textbooks say 20-50%[^5][^4]. One case firm used 19% but measured 37.8%[^7].

faq.q: Can we write off the dead stock the AI flags?
faq.a: Only once you act on it. For tax, goods must be scrapped or actually offered at a reduced price[^35][^36]. Ask your accountant well before year end.

faq.q: Will buyers still approve the orders?
faq.a: Yes, and they should: in field tests at a parts retailer, adjusting the tool's inputs added profit, while overriding its outputs cut it[^10][^8].

buyVsBuild.buy: Mostly buy, starting with what your ERP already has, then a planning add-on for several branches, lumpy parts or many suppliers[^25][^33]. Most firms now buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases were bought in 2025, up from 53%[^39].
buyVsBuild.build: Build only the narrow pieces your own data does best, such as late-order prediction from your purchase history[^14][^13]. In MIT NANDA's 2025 report, organizations' internal builds reached deployment about 33% of the time, against 67% for partnerships[^40].

pickElse: When you have a few hundred steady items in one warehouse: ERP reorder rules by ABC class, reviewed each quarter, may be enough[^28].
New items, promotions or strong seasons: fix the demand forecast first; see our AI demand forecasting guide[^26].
Counts you can't trust: fix cycle counting before you buy any planning tool[^17][^18].

Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. offer.heading: Not sure how much cash is stuck in your stock? Get a free diagnostic
offer.body: Bring us your inventory management process and a stock export. In 30 minutes we compare your stock-to-sales ratio with your sector, and you leave with the first step and a before-and-after measure. You get it in writing, with no sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Wanted to know where to start and how to measure it. The no-licence first step (lead-time and dead-stock checks on our own purchase history) was buried as recipe 3; it now leads as recipe 1. Each recipe names who does each step, and the test plan ends in cash and fill rate against the sector ratio. Time to go live is only given as vendor claims (6-12 weeks), labelled as such.

Stalled on service level, fill rate, MRP and DRP, lot-for-lot and 'probabilistic planning'. Each is now defined in plain words or swapped out. The own-data column header was too long for a phone and is now 'Months in stock, Sep 2026 (2025)'.

Asked what it does to the unit's margin and whether one branch can go first. The example now turns the carrying saving into 0.4-0.7% of sales. The live test already runs on one branch or product family beside a matched branch, and team time is covered by the 36.5% cut in ordering time from the store study. Reworded the last ERP recipe step so the 12-week check reads cleanly.

Read as head of supply chain and purchasing. Pushed back that ISM figures are buyers' reported lead times, not measured deliveries; the bottom line now says deliveries slowed 11 months running and the recipe says 'reported lead times'. Wanted the override evidence labelled by setting, so the bottom line and FAQ now say parts retailer. Buyer, planner, branch manager and controller each own a named decision, which matches how purchasing runs. No study from a mid-size distributor exists in the research, so none is claimed.

Passes the 10-second test: the title is his question and the bottom line leads with cash. Return is answered in dollars per $10M of sales; skills by a first step that needs an analyst, not a data scientist; data by the recount-first step. The offer now promises his ratio against his sector, a concrete thing to walk away with. Gaps he'd notice: no security or data-sharing guidance for add-ons and no case from a firm his size, because the research has neither; no Zavient fee is shown, per site rules. Lead's decision after review: carrying cost widened to 10-30% (APQC median to textbook range), own-data columns recomputed at both ends, and the MIT NANDA figure labelled as read from a published copy.

answers.human-role: Your buyers keep the order decision: they approve every suggested purchase order and transfer before it goes out[^11][^8]. Planners own the inputs, branch managers the transfers, and the controller any write-down[^25][^21][^35].
answers.team-after: Buyers work a ranked list of exceptions instead of scanning every item, and spend more time chasing late suppliers[^11][^14]. Planners review the override log each month against results[^10].
answers.example: At a $40M, three-branch parts distributor, AI sets safety stock from measured supplier lead times, flags dead stock and suggests branch transfers that managers approve[^1]. A 10% stock cut there would free about $880k[^1].
answers.table-1: AI sets safety stock and reorder points per item from demand and supplier lead-time swings, segments items by value and demand, and flags slow stock and branch transfers[^25][^13][^23].
answers.table-2: Your ERP may already set reorder points: NetSuite calculates them and sets safety stock by segment, while Business Central and Acumatica take safety stock typed in by hand[^24][^25][^27][^31]. Add-ons such as Smart IP&O plan from the odds of each demand level[^32].
answers.recipes: Start with lead-time and dead-stock checks on your own ERP history, then add a planning add-on only for several branches, lumpy parts or many suppliers[^3][^33]. A single warehouse on NetSuite or Business Central can tune the features it already pays for[^25][^28].
answers.own-data: Machinery distributors hold about $2.21M of stock per $10M of yearly sales, against $1.01M across all wholesalers and $608k for grocery distributors, by our math from Census ratios[^1]. By our math, a 10% cut frees a tenth of that[^1].
answers.rules: Treasury Regulation 1.471-2(c) and the Thor Power Tool ruling let you write dead stock down for tax only once you scrap it or offer it at a lower price[^35][^37]. For your books, FASB ASC 330 carries inventory at the lower of cost and net realizable value[^38].
answers.benchmark: Recount a sample of stock records, then replay the last 12 months with today's settings and with the tool's, before an 8-12 week live trial on one branch[^17][^13][^8]. Price the result in cash, fill rate and buyer hours[^1].
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI inventory management goes wrong when stock records are wrong, demand is lumpy, lead times are guessed, or buyers override outputs without logging why[^17][^26][^15][^8].
answers.something-else: Pick something else when ERP reorder rules will do, when the demand forecast is the real problem, or when you can't trust your stock counts[^28][^26][^17].
